newsitem.title: USA: World Bank anti-corruption stance lauded.
newsitem.headline: World Bank anti-corruption stance lauded.

text.p: The head of an international corruption-fighting coalition lauded the World Bank's broadside against bribery on Wednesday, and laid out his own organization's efforts in the struggle.

"Corruption has become such an important issue here, it seems Washington is turning into the epicenter of the fight against corruption," said Peter Eigen, chairman and founder of Berlin-based Transparency International.
He cited estimates that as much as 1/3 of total loans to developing countries have been wasted due to corruption.
Business people surveyed by Transparency International listed Nigeria, Pakistan, Kenya, Bangladesh and China as the worst offenders.

Although the World Bank has played some role in fighting corruption through the enforcement of procurement guidelines and financial accounting standards, Eigen said a "conscious, hands off approach," has also characterized the Bank's anti-corruption approach in the past. Now, he said, that seems to be changing.
On Tuesday, World Bank President James Wolfensohn lashed out at corruption in industrial and developing countries and vowed not to tolerate it in the projects his organization finances.

In his address to the opening plenary session of the International Monetary Fund/World Bank meeting, Wolfensohn argued that corruption diverts money from the rich to the poor and is a major barrier to economic progress in developing nations.
"Corruption is a problem that all countries have to confront," he told policymakers from the Bank's 181 member nations. "We need to deal with the cancer of corruption."
Wolfensohn's comments were echoed by IMF managing director Michel Camdessus, who also spoke at the Tuesday session.
In a book launched on Wednesday, Transparency International laid out what it called the "essential elements" that governments must follow to clean up corruption.

They include judicial system reforms, public procurement guidelines and the establishment of independent agencies to battle bribery. Transparency Internationl is planning to set up corruption-fighting workshops in individual countries based on the book.
The group is also working with governments and companies to ensure that construction and other projects are not undermined by corruption.
"We try to organize integrity pacts by which all parties agree to stop bribing," said Eigen.
He listed a $160 million refinery project in Ecuador as one successful example of this approach, and said the organization is trying to establish similar pacts in South Africa and Argentina.
